macro.title: What It Means — VWRA, Global Bonds, Gold & BTC

reads.label: VWRA (held)
reads.text: the index masks a widening split — the cloud leaders (AWS, Azure) carry it while the laggards (Apple services, Meta) drag; the diversification is inside the tape, not just across it.

reads.label: Global bonds (held)
reads.text: long yields stay high, so duration is still the sore spot; a softer dollar is a mild relief for a USD-hedged AGGU holder but the level, not the currency, is the point.

reads.label: Gold (read only)
reads.text: bid toward US$4,100 on the Gulf and an easing dollar, still well below its January peak.

reads.label: BTC (read only)
reads.text: firm near US$64.5k but on thin ETF flows — high-beta risk, not a haven. The two he holds stay VWRA and global bonds; the two he only reads stay gold and BTC.

stories.headline: The Beating Lands, and the War Finds Egypt
stories.dek: Washington answered the missile salvo with a “heavy wave” on the Revolutionary Guard; Tehran vowed to punish the aggressor the same day; and for the first time the fighting reached Egypt, where a drone set a gas terminal alight. The barrel jumped eight per cent — then faded. The market is still betting the strait stays open.

stories.headline: The First Bill Under the New Name
stories.dek: A week after energy entered the trade ministry’s title, the number that makes the point lands on the reader’s own account: household electricity is up 17 per cent this quarter, to 31.91 cents a unit — and the reason runs straight back to the gas ships burning off Egypt (p3).

stories.kicker: The Macro Desk · The Portfolio Lens
stories.headline: The Dollar Was Supposed to Rise. It Fell.
stories.dek: The Bank of Japan held but leaned hawkish, Amazon’s cloud blew past every estimate, and gold pushed toward $4,100 on the Gulf. And yet the dollar, the one thing a rate-and-war story is meant to lift, slipped a full per cent. The clean signal this week is not the Fed — it is the AI cloud pulling the tape apart.

stories.headline: Two Speeds in One Quarter
stories.dek: The HDB resale index fell for a second straight quarter — and in the same three months a record 491 flats changed hands above a million dollars. A cooling average and a heating ceiling are the same market now — which is why last week’s wait-out removal looks less like a gamble.

stories.headline: It Answers More — and Invents More
stories.dek: Kimi K3’s independent scores are in: third or fourth of 189 models, Opus-4.8-class, at a third of the price. The same testing found the catch — a hallucination rate that climbed to 51 per cent. The best open model in the world is also, by this measure, the most confidently wrong.

stories.headline: The Cheaper Sensor, and Whether You Can Train on It
stories.dek: Garmin’s CIRQA — the $200 screen-free band that undercuts Whoop’s subscription — drew its first reviews this week, and they landed on one question: it carries an older heart-rate sensor than Garmin’s own newer watches. For a reader who trains on the number, that is the whole review.

stories.headline: The Release That Kills the Port Number
stories.dek: The 2026.8 beta’s changelog is now readable ahead of next week’s release, and its most telling line is small: new installs drop the “:8123” from the address bar, and network settings move out of YAML into the interface — with a five-minute failsafe so you cannot lock yourself out. The “non-technical” Home Assistant, in concrete form.

stories.headline: A Watch You Wear to Read the World
stories.dek: A Dubai atelier has taken Perrelet’s travel GMT and hand-painted its dial into a compass rose ringed by the four corners of the globe — no two alike, fifty made, US$2,990. A lovely, honest object, sold on paint and scarcity rather than horology. Read it as education, not endorsement.

stories.headline: Every Number Is In but the One That Counts
stories.dek: Spider-Man: Brand New Day goes wide in America today, its verdict now firmed — Certified Fresh at ninety-one across a hundred and fifty-one reviews, and still the lowest of Tom Holland’s four solos. The one figure the weekend has not yet printed is the money, and everyone is guessing at it.

stories.headline: A Line Drawn, and the Fight Over Enforcing It
stories.dek: France’s under-15 social-media ban is law — but lawmakers stripped out its enforcement mechanism, and the real fight has moved to Australia, where Elon Musk’s X is challenging the crackdown. Meanwhile a large new study says the harm the bans assume is still not proven.

stories.headline: A Wind Three Hundred Thousand Light-Years Wide
stories.dek: Japan’s XRISM X-ray satellite measured the wind off a distant quasar’s black hole and found it carrying a hundred times the energy anyone had estimated — enough to stir gas across three hundred thousand light-years, far beyond the galaxy that hosts it.

stories.headline: The Deal-Breaker Is a Way of Life, Not a Ballot
stories.dek: A new experiment finds young Americans reject a date across party lines far more than they reward one within them — and the reason isn’t “bad character.” It’s the lifestyle, the values it implies, and the fear of what family and friends will say.

stories.headline: Now We Can See the Repair Crew at Work
stories.dek: A new proteomics study took muscle biopsies before and after a hard lifting session and watched what happens next: the heavy load damages the contractile proteins, and a repair network tags the damage for clearance while building fresh protein to replace it. It is the machinery behind “use it or lose it,” finally photographed.

stories.headline: The Week the Alarms Go Off
stories.dek: Two of the autumn’s biggest on-sales land in the same August week — sumo tickets on the 8th, BIGBANG’s presale on the 11th — and MAMAMOO plays tonight. Set the alarms; the good seats do not wait.

stories.headline: The Admiral’s Bargain
stories.dek: In 1911 Winston Churchill chose to run the Royal Navy on oil it did not have instead of the coal it did — trading British security for foreign speed, and buying an oil company to cover the risk. Every leap in power since has struck the same bargain. This week’s version runs on electricity, and the reader is paying its first instalment.
